newsitem.title: CANADA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-MESSIER SIGNS WITH VANCOUVER, SPURNING NEW YORK.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-MESSIER SIGNS WITH VANCOUVER, SPURNING NEW YORK.

text.p: Mark Messier, who led the New Yorngers to their first Stanley Cup in 54 years in 1994, is moving on after signing an extremely lucrative three-year deal on Monday with the Vancouver Canucks.

Terms were not disclosed, but various reports said the 36-year-old former Ranger captain's deal was worth at least $20 million and included an incentive package that could make it substantially richer.
"It's always tough to make changes, but changes are about great opportunities as well," Messier said at a news conference. "Hopefully, I can come here and help Vancouver win the Stanley Cup."

Messier, considered one of the best leaders in North American team sports, had 36 goals and 48 assists for 84 points last season in the final year of a three-year, $18 million contract with the Rangers, with whom he played six seasons.
Canucks president and general manager Pat Quinn said: "We haven't been able to realise our dream of winning the Stanley Cup and we signed Mark to teach us how to win."
He added: "As many of you know it's not talent alone that wins the Stanley Cup. When I think of Mark I don't think just of his scoring, I think of him as a winner.
"I think of the steel jaw, the eyes set. It's a long tough road to the Stanley Cup, but Mark will allow us to get a little closer to our goal."
"It's a sad day in New York," Madison Square Garden President Dave Checketts said in a radio interview.
"I wanted him to finish his career in New York. We thought there was a level of trust that clearly did not exist. We did not get a chance to make one last pitch. We never made our best offer."
"Leaving New York was one of the toughest things I had to do," said Messier, "but I thought it was best for me to move on."
Rangers general manager Neil Smith said: "This is the hardest thing that has happened to me as Ranger general manager. I misread this. We wanted Mark back.
"He never got back to me." The Rangers had offered about $10 million for years with an option for the third.
"He said he wanted to stay in New York but his actions were different. If you believe what he said, he wanted to stay here. You have to believe what a person says, don't you?"
"I had no reservations at all moving back to Canada," said Messier. "Actually, it was an attraction to me being a Canadian to finish my career here."

The Canucks get a double dose of revenge along with their new player. They lost to the Rangers in the 1994 Stanley Cup Finals and lost again to New York in the Wayne Gretzky sweepstakes last summer when the Rangers signed The Great One, Messier's former Edmonton teammate.

However, there has been speculation that some in the Rangers' organisation privately might not mind losing Messier since it would give full control of the team to coach Colin Campbell, who received a contract extension earlier this month.
The Canucks missed the playoffs last season by going 35-40-7 for 77 points, and had trouble filling GM Place, their new arena.

Messier could be just the player to bring out the best in inconsistent star Russian wingers Pavel Bure and Alexander Mogilny. The Canucks now can boast two top lines that will include, among others, Messier, Bure, Mogilny and the current team captain, Trevor Linden.
In 18 NHL seasons with Edmonton and the Rangers, Messier is 10th all-time in goals with 575, sixth in assists with 977 and fifth in points with 1,552.

A ferocious two-way player, Messier won the Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff Most Valuable Player for the Oilers in 1984. He also won the Hart Trophy, given to the league's MVP, in 1990 with Edmonton and 1992 with the Rangers.
Messier teamed with Gretzky on the Oilers dynasty of the 1980s, but also led Edmonton to the 1990 Stanley Cup after Gretzky's departure.

Though he suffered through one of the worst playoff performances of his career last season, scoring three goals with nine assists in 15 games, Messier is still second to Gretzky among all-time post-season performers with 109 goals, 186 assists and 295 points.
Messier ended the Rangers' 50-year-old Stanley Cup "curse" less than three years after joining the team.

With the Rangers trailing three games to two in the 1994 semifinals, he guaranteed a victory in Game 6 in New Jersey, and had a natural hat trick in the third period to ensure it. The Rangers won the seventh game in double overtime and went on to defeat the Canucks in seven games to win the Cup.
